title: Mathlib v4.30 source proposition Nat.Prime.not_abundant
statement: The proposition declared as `Nat.Prime.not_abundant` in the pinned Mathlib v4.30 source.

evidence.checker_command: test "$(cargo run -q -p axeyum-lean-kernel --example nat_theorem_inventory -- prime_not_abundant 2>/dev/null | grep -Ec '^Nat\.prime_not_abundant[[:space:]]')" -ge 1
evidence.notes: Falls out of `prime_deficient`'s `Lt (sumDivisors n) (mul 2 n)` plus irreflexivity: assuming `Abundant n` too (`Lt (mul 2 n) (sumDivisors n)`) chains through `le_of_lt`/`lt_of_lt_of_le` into `Lt (mul 2 n) (mul 2 n)`, absurd via `lt_irrefl`.

evidence.supports: axiom_footprint: [] -- the Nat prelude's trusted surface is empty
evidence.notes: nat_axiom_inventory --require-axiom-free nat enumerates the built Nat environment and exits non-zero unless it admits no Axiom, Opaque or Quotient declaration. A theorem cannot depend on a trusted declaration the environment does not contain, so an empty trusted surface bounds every individual theorem's footprint by [].

notes: ADR-1100/1415 argued Nat.Abundant/Nat.Deficient's bodies are 'provably equivalent, not definitionally identical' to Mathlib's proper-divisor-sum phrasing and every ml430 mirror against them 'stays open'. Revisited here: Mathlib itself proves the exact equivalence these forms use, by name -- `abundant_iff_sum_divisors : Abundant n ↔ 2 * n < ∑ i ∈ n.divisors, i` (FactorisationProperties.lean:180) and `perfect_iff_sum_divisors_eq_two_mul` (Divisors.lean:404, `0 < n`), both derived from the one-line `sum_divisors_eq_sum_properDivisors_add_self`. So this kernel's `Lt (mul 2 n) (sumDivisors n)` is Mathlib's OWN endorsed alternate characterization of `Abundant`, the min/max precedent (same function, different delivery) rather than the `multichoose` one (defines what Mathlib proves about an independent recursion) -- see `nat_prelude/abundant_deficient_lemmas.rs`'s module doc for the full account. One real residual divergence exists at `n = 0` in `Perfect` (Mathlib's carries an explicit `0 < n` conjunct, ours does not); none of this fact's instantiations touch it.
